scope.title: History view
scope.framing: The Specs a history view rests on, in reading order. A history view is a read model whose row folds the events of several streams, such as the order allocation history of the example domain. The history projection comes first because it pins the form, its fold and that view; the projection contract and the read models follow with the row conventions and the read-model rules every view shares. The rebuild, the history rebuild with its five examples, the write pause and the generation registry say how such a view comes to exist and is rebuilt while the commands that write its sources are refused. The rebuild comes first because it holds the operator entries and the batch chain both paths share; the history rebuild holds the paused path alone and the five examples verify it, so the rebuild's implementation binding claims the online path and the history rebuild shows the paused path designed apart from it. The example domain names the events the view folds, and the command declaration and the command pipeline bind the view to the commands that feed it and write it inside each command. The event envelope, the journal and the queries are where the events come from on the live path and on the backfill, and D9 is the decision that a read model which depends on history across several streams rebuilds under a write pause.

questions.question: Extension E-8: the doc names a generation registry, a marker and a gate without their shapes, and says to keep the old generation for a rollback period without saying whether live commands keep writing it; the option taken here is the `generations` table below with seven states, a rollback period of 7 days, one generation being built per read model at a time, and a retired generation that is kept and not written, so that a rollback reopens it as `verifying`, one verify pass repairs what the writes since its retirement changed, and the ordinary switch makes it active again; a rollback is therefore a verify pass and then a switch of one write, never one write by itself (E-8, D9, Sc L2-5)

Extension E-8, reach of a generation: the doc says nothing about tenants and rebuild; one generation per read model spans every tenant, the registry has no tenant dimension, one row is active for all tenants and the batches iterate the tenant list of `spec:command.actor-and-scope`; the registry is operational data of the deployment, so its indexes lead with the read model name and not with `tenantId`, a confirmed deviation from Law 11's index rule of the same kind the obligation module records under E-57, while every table that holds tenant data, the read-model rows among them, leads with the tenant; a rebuild for one tenant is not offered (E-8, D9, D11, Law 11, E-57)

Extension E-42, as it touches the registry: a restore brings back a generation row and its progress row at their checkpoint and drops the scheduled batch that was driving them, so the row's fence at inventory time is the restore's proof that the generation is still stranded, and `resumeChain` bumping it is the proof that it is not (E-42, F12)

Extension E-8, the first generation: the doc says how a generation is rebuilt and not how a read model's first generation comes to exist; the option taken here is that a read model is installed through its first rebuild, generation 1 starting as `building` like any other, so a read model added to a deployment that has history serves that history from its first switch and no transition claims coverage it did not build; a command that finds no generation to write fails as a technical failure and a query that finds no active generation fails the same way (E-8, D9, D19)

Extension E-40, the checkpoint: the cursor, the batch size and the counts live on the progress row and not on the generation row, because a batch that wrote its checkpoint on the row every command reads would re-run every command in flight on the read model once per batch; the progress row is the one checkpoint of every batch whatever drives it (E-40, F1)

Extension E-49, as it touches the registry: on a deployment whose grants predate the tenant list the list is empty while grants exist, and a generation started then visits no tenant; the option taken here is that `startGeneration` refuses then, with a message naming `fillTenants`, the operator entry of `spec:application.rebuild` that fills the list from the grants, and refuses while that fill runs (E-49, E-8, Law 11)

Extension E-9, the history fold: D2 orders events only within a stream, and the two paths feed one history row in different orders, the live path command by command and the backfill stream by stream; the option taken here is a fold that gives one row whatever the order across streams and however its events are split between calls, a row no fold deletes, which keeps its subject's ended state, and baselines dropped before `keyOf`, so a view whose meaning needs the order across streams waits for the ordered consumer of D18 (E-9, D2, D9, D18, E-25)

The cost of the binding on the live path, one row read and one write of up to `rowBudgetBytes` per command and the measure of the row, is taken by the first experiment's latency cell with the order allocation history bound, for `PlaceOrder` and for `CancelOrder` of an order of the maximum lines, before the view is declared essential anywhere (E-9, E-47, F13)

Extension E-9, the check of the history fold: the order independence the Contract requires is checked for the order allocation history alone; the option taken here is that every history projection of an application carries a pure test that folds a sample of one key's events in every interleaving of its streams and every split into calls, and a library helper that runs that test is added with a second history view (E-9, D2, D18)

A history row keeps a deleted subject's history and every rebuild writes it again from the journal; whether a history view falls under the retention and deletion policy of D19, and what its rebuild does after an erasure, is answered by that policy (D19, D9, E-9)

Extension E-40, the shape of a history batch: a batch takes one stream, so a pass costs at least one scheduled mutation per source stream and the pause lasts about twice the stream count times one batch; the alternative is a batch that takes streams from one `list` page until its event budget is spent, one `history` call per stream, with the byte bound counting one baseline per stream; the first paused rebuild on the native backend measures one batch, and the shape is chosen with that number (E-40, E-9, F13, F19, D9)

The verify pass under the write pause: a history view's generation is built while no source changes, so its verify pass repeats the backfill's batches and, by `spec:application.history-rebuild#design.historyVerify`, finds nothing over a covered generation, which doubles the pause; the option kept here is the pass, as D9's "Verify coverage, then switch" and Sc L2-6's "writes reopen only after verification" read, and whether a paused generation is `verified` when its backfill ends is the owner's (D9, Sc L2-6, OD-157)

Whether a history view's batch chain, at up to 2 MiB of rows per batch scheduled with `runAfter(0)`, is held by the deployment class's write throughput limit, `spec:facts.f13-transactions-have-limits#design.limitWriteThroughput`, which the first paused rebuild on the native backend and one hosted run show (F13, E-40)

Must every source's migration that reads history finish before `startGeneration` closes its source scopes, with abort, migration completion and a fresh generation as the recovery if it did not? If enumeration must instead remain possible during that migration, which context query provides it without constructing a DTO of the wrong meaning?

Should the native-backend abort example inject failure in the second source's audit insert, assert unchanged generation, progress, gate entries and audit records, then retry after removing the fault and assert one successful abort with both sources reopened? The same atomicity check should cover the switch that reopens them.

Should the native-backend example use two tenants with equal local order and stock item IDs, check their folds separately, and refuse a command that writes a paused source without a history binding in both tenants, while a command writing only an unrelated source remains allowed? Include a retry of resume after its response is lost so the same saved event page cannot change the fold twice.

Extension E-46: the second lifecycle command, the essential summary, the command that creates stock, the unit price an order line carries, the bound on an order line's stock item ID, the rejection reasons, the stream budgets of the two stream types, the order of the two context calls and the history-dependent view Sc L2-6 builds are choices the doc leaves open; two of them are decided, that the stock item keeps totals only and `release` takes its quantities from the cancelled order's own lines, and that the order allocation history view stays in the experiment; the owner may substitute the others, and the experiment's terms move with them (E-46, E-2, E-9, First experiment)

Extension E-9: the doc says a projection is named, versioned and deterministic and that live update and rebuild share its logic; it does not give the signature or the row shape, for counts and sums it names the marker but not the aggregate row, and for the read models that depend on history across several streams, the ones the write pause exists for, it names no input. The option taken here: a per-entity read model declared as a `ReadModel<D, Row>` with `name`, `table`, `rowBudgetBytes` and its `projections`, a list of `Projection<D, Row>` with the latest first, each holding `version`, `keyOf` and `project` alone, rows with `tenantId`, `generation`, `key`, `projectionVersion` and `sourceVersions`, one `applyProjection` helper with a mode per caller that writes each generation by its role, active, building or verifying, with the projection whose version the generation records, for the aggregate form the row and the writer `spec:application.aggregate-projection` pins, and for a history-dependent view a `HistoryProjection<Row>` that folds events into the prior row, fed on the live path by the events the operation appended, which the adapter's `streams` entry carries, and on the backfill by the context's `history` pages under the write pause, with `sourceVersions` recording the highest version folded per stream so that an event is never folded twice; a row that derives from more than one source stream type is a history row, its projection bound once per source stream type, and a small cross-context view of current state is D8's parent query over bounded component reads; the owner confirms the three forms and has not ruled on the split of a per-entity read model into `ReadModel` and `Projection`, on the write by generation role or on the row measured against its budget at every write (E-9, E-23, E-24, D8, D9)

Extension E-9, two projection versions: the doc says live update and rebuild share one projection and does not say how a command writes two generations built by two versions; the option taken here is that a read model declares its projection versions as a list, the latest first, and `applyProjection` writes each generation with the projection whose version the generation row records, failing as a technical failure when the read model declares none of that version, so the rows of one generation are one truth of one version; the cost is that an earlier version stays in the code while a generation that records it is written or can be rolled back to, and a projection changed without a version change is still undetected (E-9, D8, D9)

The rule that a row with a newer version is never overwritten is read as the backfill path's rule only, so a live write to the active generation always lands, as `step3` has it; the owner has not confirmed that reading (D9, E-9)

Extension E-9, a composite row of current state: D8 lets a small cross-context view be a read model updated in the command, and no form here writes one row from the DTOs of two sources, because `project` builds a whole row from one DTO and a backfill enumerates one source; the option taken here is D8's other default, a parent query over bounded component reads, until a view needs such a row, which then needs a form whose `project` takes the DTO of every matching entry of one command and whose backfill reads the other context in the same mutation, online (E-9, D8, E-45)

Extension E-9, the cost of `sourceVersions`: a history row's entries repeat the row's tenant ID once per source stream, about three quarters of the largest order allocation history row by `spec:application.history-projection#design.tableOrderAllocationHistory`; whether a row's `sourceVersions` may omit `tenantId`, equal to the row's on every entry, and the write rule compare three identity fields, is a choice the owner may take with the pinned conventions (E-9, Law 11, F13)

Probe 5 showed that the built-in `.paginate` treats `maximumRowsRead` as advice once a page has an end cursor and that a cursor it issued is refused by any other query, so a subscription over the active generation threw `InvalidCursor` at a switch; a parent list therefore pages with `paginator` of `convex-helpers`, as a context list does, and a pinned page is bounded on every run by the row cap and by the byte cap as `spec:context.queries` states it, the helper stopping at the row that reaches it and admitting that row whole, and answers `SplitRequired` beyond them (Probe 5, F13, D8, D9)

Extension E-24, as it reaches read models: a list over a parent read-model table calls `paginator` of `convex-helpers` with the options of `boundedPage`, a row cap of twice the item cap, with each cursor of the client's pair moved into the active generation by `pageInGeneration`, and returns through `paginationResultValidator` with its rows mapped by `readModelView`, and a client pages every list by an explicit cursor pair with no hook; these are options taken here and the owner has not ruled (E-24, S4, Probe 5, D8)

Extension E-6, as it reaches queries: a parent query establishes and authorizes its actor through `authorizeQuery`, and its refusal is the command's rejection shape, `RejectionData` with the query's name in the field `entry` and the codes `unauthenticated` or `forbidden`; the owner confirmed the word, and nothing else of the shape is new (E-6, D7, D11, Law 5)
Probe 3 pending: the cost of one component call in latency and function-call quota decides whether one entity's detail stays a component query or hot reads move, which is OQ1 (Probe 3, F4, OQ1)

Extension E-45: the doc says a small cross-context view is a parent query over bounded component reads and does not give the bound; the option taken here is at most 8 component reads per parent query and at most 4 read-model rows written per command, both measured by the first experiment (E-45, D8)

Extension E-9, as it reaches read models: D8 lets a small cross-context view be a parent query over bounded component reads or a read model updated in the command; the option taken here is the parent query for a view of current state, because no form of `spec:application.projection-contract` writes one row from the DTOs of two sources, and the history projection for a view that folds the events of several streams; a composite row of current state is a form for the view that needs it (E-9, E-45, D8)

`@convex-dev/migrations` walks only the tables of the component it is defined in, reaches a context's rows only through a parent internal mutation written by hand against a contract its README does not document and the compiled tier needs a cast for, keeps a status apart from the generation's state, and leaves no error on its row when a batch fails past the read limit, so every batch is driven by the rebuild's own self-scheduled internal mutation and the progress row is the one checkpoint; a hosted deployment and sustained contention are not observed (Probe 6, F1, F17, D9)

Extension E-40: the doc binds resumable batching to `@convex-dev/migrations` and gives no batch size; the component iterates a parent table while the sources of a read model live in a context component. The option taken here: a batch is one mutation with one cursor on the progress row and a bound of at most 100 entities, capped by the read model's declared `rowBudgetBytes` so that the parent's point reads and writes stay under 4 MiB, and by the context's byte-derived `list` page bound, which is 16 items at the default 256 KiB stream budget; every batch, the backfill and the verify pass over a context's enumeration and the purge over a parent table, is driven by the platform's own self-scheduled internal mutation, and the rebuild uses the component for nothing, because Probe 6 showed that it walks only the tables of the component it is defined in and drives a context's rows only through a parent internal mutation written by hand against a contract its README does not document; the progress row is the one checkpoint (E-40, E-24, E-9, F17, F13, F1)

Extension E-8: the registry states, the rollback period, what a rollback does, the gate document, the scope a paused rebuild closes and the reach of a generation are design choices the doc does not make; they are pinned in the two contracts under this workflow (E-8, E-9, E-38, D9)

Extension E-8, what this workflow does not offer: the online path is pinned for a per-entity read model with one source stream type and the paused path for a history view, a `HistoryRebuildTarget` with its sources, in `spec:application.history-rebuild`; the aggregate form's rebuild is deferred with the form in its own Spec, the aggregate projection, and a row made from the current state of more than one source has no form at all, as `spec:application.projection-contract` records; `rollbackGeneration` refuses a generation that needs a write pause, because nothing would hold its sources while live commands fold onto a row that missed the events since its retirement, so such a view returns to earlier rules only through a new generation under the pause (E-8, E-9, D9, D18)

Extension E-49, a deployment whose grants predate the tenant list: the tenant list is written by `insertGrant`, so on such a deployment it holds no row while `grants` holds many, and a pass over an empty list visits no tenant and still ends; the option taken here is that `startGeneration` refuses an empty list beside a grant with a message naming `fillTenants`, and `fillTenants`, an operator entry, walks the grants in bounded batches through a progress row of its own and inserts each missing tenant once; a list that holds a tenant whose first grant came after the table and misses an older one is not detected by that refusal, so the operator runs `fillTenants` on such a deployment before its first `startGeneration` (E-49, E-48, E-40, Law 11)

Extension E-8: the doc names a maintenance gate every writer reads, fencing or draining of background writers, and operator resume and abort; the option taken here is one gate document per deployment holding the closed scopes, each in one `closed` state, with no fence of its own and no drain interval, because optimistic concurrency serializes every writer's gate read against the close and the generation row's fence already fences a rebuild's batches, and a refusal answered with `writePaused`, the transient code the outcome boundary reserves for this contract under its E-35, which this contract confirms; the scope a paused rebuild closes is the paused view's sources, one `source:` entry per context and stream type its bindings name, because a consistent cut must hold every writer of those streams and a use case that writes a source stream without maintaining the view would otherwise pass the gate, which is why the command declaration names what it writes under E-38 and the pipeline proves the list at its step 9; an operator entry closes only a tenant or `all`, the coarser and always safe scopes, and no scope names a read model, because nothing would close it (E-8, E-38, D9, D4, F1)

Extension E-8, the generation exemption: a batch reads the gate with the scopes `all` and its tenant, and no entry of either scope ever names a generation, so the exemption `gateAllows` makes for a given generation is reached by no reader; either the exemption goes, or a history batch reads the gate with its source scopes as well and passes them by it (E-8, D9)

Should its operating instructions distinguish a stopped pass from a verified generation awaiting switch, using `getGenerations` and `getGate`, and measure the closed interval through the successful switch or abort? Keep any acceptable pause length for the owner's decision rather than deriving a timeout from a batch estimate.

Extension E-7: the doc says a small composition helper and shared schema values; the helper signatures, the executor signature and the read-model binding below are the design's; the cost is two registered mutations per command instead of one, and the cheaper alternative the design refuted is one public export per command plus one generic internal dispatcher mutation keyed by command type, as D7's conditional dispatcher already does; it lost because trusted server callers would then reach every command through one untyped `internalMutation`, so a renamed handler or a broken argument contract would pass `tsc` at the caller and fail only at runtime, which is the check Sc L2-4 exists to keep before traffic, and because the receipt fingerprint's contract version would be looked up by string rather than typed; the owner may still prefer the dispatcher form once code generation makes the per-command internal entry free (E-7, D12, D7, Sc L2-4, Decision method rule 5)

Extension E-7: the pipeline receives the declaration and takes the fingerprint's contract version from it, and the type check at a typed caller is the check of Sc L2-4, so no standing map from command type to declaration exists; the conditional dispatcher of `spec:command.outcome-boundary` is the one thing that would need such a map and brings it with it; this is a provisional reading the owner rules (E-7, D12, D18, OQ2)

Extension E-38: the doc names five declaration fields; this design adds `contractVersion` for the fingerprint, `retention` and `irreversible` for receipts, `admission`, `bounds`, `rejections`, `audit`, `diagnosticSink` and `writes`, each serving a cited rule of another Spec, and asks whether the owner accepts them as part of the one declaration; `bounds` is the one input bound in the corpus, `maxItems` and `maxBytes`, checked by the pipeline's step 1 and by no executor body, so `spec:application.parent-use-cases` reads it rather than declaring a bound of its own; `writes` is required on every declaration, because an absent list would be an unchecked one, and `readModels` is optional, absent meaning none, which the owner has not ruled; `writes` names the context and stream type pairs the executor may write, from which the pipeline's step 7 derives the source scopes the write pause closes for a consistent cut and which step 9 proves against the `streams` entries the executor returns, because a use case that writes a source stream without maintaining the paused view would otherwise pass the gate; the declaration still imports nothing from the obligation family, so a command's static reactions are not a field here but the `createObligation` calls of its executor, as `spec:obligations.fan-out-and-chains` rules under E-54 (E-38, E-8, E-54, D6, D9, D10, D19, Thesis)

Extension E-30: the doc names the outcome, the operation ID and the affected stream versions as what a command returns, but not a wire shape; the shape here is a union discriminated by `replayed`, whose executed member carries the declaration's result and whose replayed member carries `result` null because a receipt stores no result, so the entry's returns validator admits a replay as a value; affected IDs are application IDs, never private document IDs (E-30, D2, D6, D8)

Extension E-31: the doc says an operation's ID ties together everything one request caused but not how it is minted, and it says a derived command carries causation and an event's `causedBy` may be a triggering event without saying how that cause reaches the pipeline; here the pipeline mints the operation ID once per top-level mutation with `crypto.randomUUID()` before the first context call, a duplicate returns the operation ID stored on the receipt, and the internal entry takes an optional `causedBy` argument that step 7 copies onto the `OperationRef` when present, so a reaction that issues a derived command passes `causedBy` of kind `event` naming its publication event and the envelope's `event` variant has exactly one producer, while an entry called without it mints `causedBy` of kind `command` from the declaration's name; the obligation and attempt behind a derived command are found through its receipt, whose request key is the obligation's effect key, and never through the envelope (E-31, E-54, D2, D13, Vocab: operation)

Extension E-32: the doc places rate admission for new intent after the duplicate check and makes a rate or capacity refusal a retryable error, but names no admission mechanism; here admission is an optional per-command policy in the declaration, absent by default, evaluated inside the mutation so that a refusal that throws leaves no consumption behind; the flip side is that a consumption the policy writes commits only with the command, so the policy counts committed intent and cannot bound refused or unauthorized traffic, and a product that must bound refused traffic needs the dispatcher form of D7, where the parent survives the body's rejection (E-32, D4, D6, D7)

Extension E-33: the doc lists the callers that need receipts and leaves UI commands to the client guarantee; here a public caller may still supply a request key to opt into a receipt, which Probe 1 showed a caller of `ConvexHttpClient` needs when it retries, and the internal entry always requires one (E-33, D6, Probe 1)

Probe 4 showed on the pinned backend that the transaction limits are one budget across the parent and its component sub-transactions, so the per-command bounds are checked against one budget; `ctx.runMutation` accepts a `transactionLimits` option, the design passes none on a context call, and whether a call should reserve room with it for the work after it stays open (Probe 4, F13, S3)

Extension E-9: the doc says essential read models are updated inside the command and does not say from what or in what order; here step 9 writes a per-entity read model from the DTO of each matching `streams` entry, never from its events, and a history read model from the events of every matching entry in one call per command, checks `writes` first, then that each bound read model has a generation to write, then the count of the rows it writes against `limitReadModelWritesPerCommand`, each failure a plain error, and the library helpers that step 9 calls are generic over the application's data model; the owner has not ruled on any of it (E-9, E-7, E-8, E-45, D8, D9)

Extension E-34: step 1 bounds every text field a caller sets beside the input, the tenant ID, the request key, the correlation ID, the actor's fields and the fields of `causedBy`, in UTF-8 bytes as `limitCallText` lists them, as rejection `invalidInput`, and treats a declaration name above `limitIdLength` as a defect, a plain error, because these fields become fields of the receipt row or of every event's envelope; the doc says events stay small and names no number; the owner has not ruled (E-34, D6, D12, D19)
